The paper provides an in context learning method for tabular data. The reviews unanimously agree that the paper is well written and easy to follow. They appreciated the thorough experiments conducted, demonstrating the value of the methods, .e.g. A8ss: “The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering 203 datasets across five different benchmarks with proper statistical analysis including critical difference diagrams.”. In addition to the promising bottom-line performance, the reviews mentioned the paper provides valuable core components: A8ss “The multi-modal embedding approach is sensible .. the architectural modifications to TabPFN are well-motivated”, zDEh “The work proposes architectural choices and training schemes that maybe useful for future related works.”. These comments suggest the method is not only practical but contains insights that would be interesting to the NeurIPS community.  

In terms of weaknesses, some reviews raised an issue of novelty, as some of the elements used in the method presented here are reused from other papers. In the discussions this is agreed to be a minor issue, as the provided model has sufficiently many novel aspects. Finally, the reviews raised the need for additional experiments, but these were provided in the rebuttal phase and all major concerns are mitigated.  

Integrating the rebuttal content into the paper seems quite simple to me and the resulting paper is agreed by all reviewers to be of high quality, and a good addition to NeurIPS.

With the Author-Reviewer discussion period about to come to an end, we wanted to thank you again for the helpful feedback, and check if we have been able to address all your questions with our response above.

Thank you for your answer! 

To address your questions: 

First, we have collected more detailed per-benchmark statistics which we added to the Appendix:

|                  | #tasks | #classification | #regression | %object | %category | %bool | %float | %int | %dates |
|------------------|-----------|--------------------|----------------|-------------|---------------|-----------|------------|----------|------------|
| CARTE        |        51 |                 11 |             40 |       80.74 |          0    |        0  |      19.04 |     0.22 |       0    |
| OpenML-CC18  |        72 |                 72 |              0 |        0.05 |         7.85  |        0  |      55.80  |    22.70  |       0    |
| OpenML-CTR23 |        35 |                  0 |             35 |        0.95 |         3.91  |        0  |      66.19 |    16.91 |       0    |
| TabReD       |         8 |                  3 |              5 |        0.14 |          0    |     0.05  |      89.95 |     9.41 |     0.44   |
| TALENT-tiny  |        37 |                 26 |             11 |       12.77 |          0    |     0.44  |      63.63 |    23.15 |       0    |

As expected, all benchmarks but CARTE are very numerics-heavy, whereas CARTE only has 20% numerical columns on average.

Regarding meaningful column names in the benchmarks: this is an interesting question, but one that is very hard to tackle systematically at scale (without manually checking every dataset). Our semantic ablation, enriching column names with additional LLM-generated descriptions, suggests that the column names of the datasets within CARTE are already reasonably descriptive. Extending this to the other benchmarks could be a – albeit very indirect – way to measure this. However, given the computational resources needed, we would argue this to be too much effort for potentially too few insights. If you are aware of an easier approach to measure this, we would be happy to try it out!

To your last point: As shown, ConTextTab shines in the presence of textual/semantic data, and again, the statistics above confirm that such data is very prevalent in the CARTE benchmark, whereas it is not well represented in the other benchmarks tested on. Further refining the dataset characteristics most predictive for ConTextTab's performance is an interesting idea, but, again, we fail to see a systematic way to do so, in addition to the ablations and evaluations already provided.

We hope to have successfully addressed all of your questions!

Thank you for your quick response and the good discussion!

## Regarding discrepancies/differences in the new results table as compared to the initially submitted one

Differences in numbers stem from the following:
  - For tree baselines and RealMLP: Updating to HPO-CV ensemble.
  - For TabPFN: Updating to v2.1.0 which uses an updated model checkpoint for classification.
  - **For all R2 scores**: as mentioned in our answer to Rev. qbCU, we have changed evaluation to use a soft-clipped R2 score as severe negative outliers had a large effect on the mean score. Hence, the reported R2 numbers have changed even for models that we did not reevaluate. Newly reported R2 scores should be equal or larger to previously reported ones (as only negative scores are affected by soft-clipping).

All other scores, in particular accuracy scores of non-reevaluated baselines, should not have changed.
Does this address your observation or did we miss a discrepancy in the numbers (double-checking, we couldn’t find one)?

## Comment
We agree that the newly added, extensively tuned and ensembled baselines make the evaluation on non-semantic benchmarks more nuanced! In particular, it requires analysing the newly added per-benchmark CD diagrams, win ratio, and p-value matrices as opposed to simply comparing aggregated accuracy/r2 or rank. However, with the help of this analysis, as also laid out in more detail in our previous answer to your review as well as the one by Rev. qbCU, we see that there is no statistically significant differences on non-semantic benchmarks. This holds true in particular between TabPFN and our approach, but also for the best-performing model and our approach on every benchmark except OpenML-CTR23 (where our model is not statistically significantly worse than the second-best model), as well as across all benchmarks combined. 

Finally, we agree with Rev. qbCU (thanks for chiming in!): we could have focused solely on CARTE but wanted to highlight that increased performance on semantically rich data does not come at the cost of performance on non-semantic benchmarks. Despite this argument now being more nuanced, we think our results as outlined above show it to remain true. We understand and agree with the concerns raised by you regarding performance on non-semantic benchmarks and will make sure to not overstate this in the paper. In fact, also in our initial submission, our abstract reads

`[…]  our model is competitive with SOTA across a broad set of benchmarks while setting a new standard on the semantically rich CARTE benchmark
`

which we argue to remain true. We have updated Section 5, including the paragraph you have highlighted, taking the new results into account and adding more nuance to the discussion on the performance on non-semantic benchmarks! 

Thanks again for highlighting and giving us the chance to improve the paper in this regard!

Dear authors,

Thank you for your thorough rebuttal and engagement with reviewers. After reviewing both your responses and other reviewers' comments, I have decided to increase my score from 3 to 4, though some concerns remain:

**Question:** I noticed discrepancies in R2 and ACC metrics between the rebuttal and the manuscript for certain models/datasets. Could you clarify if these are typos or results from new experiments?

**Comment:** The new HPO CV results present a different picture than initially shown: RealMLP, CatBoost, and LightGBM now outperform ConTexTab on average. While ConTexTab shows superior performance on CARTE, this is expected given the dataset's semantic nature and your model's design. Your manuscript states: *"Our model performs particularly well for the semantically rich CARTE benchmark, highlighting the importance of incorporating semantic understanding into tabular ICL."* However, this claim is weakened by TabPFN's superior performance both on average and across other datasets. The evidence suggests that your approach offers improvements only for specific types of datasets while potentially degrading performance on others.

My decision to increase the score rests mainly on the potential practical applications: real-world datasets, with their rich semantic content, may benefit more from your approach than the academic benchmarks used in this study.

Thank you for response and for **acknowledging that we managed to address all of your questions**.

Let us first address your new questions:
We are using AutoGluon v1.2 with a time limit of 4h per task, whereas we use 50 rounds of HPO for all HPO and HPO-CV baselines combined with one final full retraining of the incumbants, as stated in Appendix B.1. Hence, HPO-CV variants can take much longer than 4h to train.

Next, **as currently formulated, we do not share your new concerns regarding AutoGluon** (the results of which have not changed since our initial submission). Like you point out, AutoGluon represents an approach very different to tabular ICL (i.e., stacking and ensembling a multitude of model architectures, making use of their respective strengths, combined with extensive per-dataset tuning), whereas our core contribution is the successful integration of high-level semantics into a table-native ICL model. To this end, through extensive evaluation, we show that our model performs on-par to existing approaches on non-semantic benchmarks while significantly outperforming all (single-architecture) models on the semantically rich CARTE benchmark, even those that are extensively tuned per dataset. With our newly added semantic ablation, we further substantiate this point. 

Looking more closely at the comparison to AutoGluon, while AutoGluon indeed outperforms our method on CARTE, given the win rate of 65% and a p-value of 0.03, the differences are not as significant as they might appear from the average scores presented in Table. Furthermore, while RealMLP, in the extensively tuned and ensembled variant, constitutes a very strong baseline, it does not significantly outperform AutoGluon on the non-semantic benchmarks as can be seen from our newly added win-ratio and p-value plots. Taken together, while the difference in performance to AutoGluon might well point to potential headroom for continued improvements of table-native ICL methods such as ours (this would be great of course!), **we fail to see how this observation contradicts our main claims or weakens our contribution.**



Naturally, we’d be very happy to discuss these points further to see if there are some aspects of your argument that we’re missing or can better address. We therefore wanted to double check if it was indeed your intention to submit your final Mandatory Acknowledgement before we had a chance to engage with your new points – we would have loved to continue the discussion!

Thank you for acknowledging our efforts and raising your score! We appreciate it!

Here are some more answers :)

## TabRed splits
We use the default (time-ordered) train/val/test splits defined by TabRed. For the HPO-CV variants we then concatenate train+val and do inner cross validation effectively ignoring the time ordering of the train/val dataset. As stated, TabReD also offers “sliding-window splits”. However, then you would evaluate exclusively the past for some splits, which also might skew performance. Given the good performance of the baselines on TabRed (and looking into the reference you stated) we agree that our current protocol is likely sufficient.

## Equation (2), attention
We apply the same special attention mechanism as in the default TabPFNv2-style cross-row attention. That is, each query vector attends to itself and the context vectors. Queries do not attend to one another, whereas context vectors can attend to each other.

## Time measurement
That’s a good point! We agree, there is no single best way to do this. Doing it on real data removes this implicit bias. However, due to the different data sizes at hand (and, e.g., the quadratic scaling of the transformer-based models), the time measurements will likely be rather spread out. Assuming a Gaussian distribution and reporting mean (or mean+std) might then give a false impression of the actual distribution, which is why we opted for a controlled way of specifying the table size. 

## Semantic secret sauce
Yes, all baselines use (our slightly adapted) AutoGluon feature processor with TF-IDF. We have experimented with LLM embeddings and baselines (GBDTs but also DL methods such as TabPFN) in the past (e.g. embedding categorical and free-text features using an LLM and then downsampling the embedding vectors to the first N PCA components, treating them as numerical features). Results indicated slight boosts for GBDTs and, to some extent, for TabPFN, but results were overall limited which is why we didn’t follow up with a systematic ablation/investigation, given also the compute overhead involved. Furthermore, for datasets with many categorial/text features, you quickly end up with very wide tables and models need to be able to handle those high-dimensional embeddings to retain the semantic information. But maybe it is a good starting point for future evaluations!

Hence, as of now, we believe the native handling of high-dimensional semantic embeddings, as opposed to ‘rolling them out’ in the feature dimension, together with the real-world data pretraining, is what sets ConTextTab apart. So, to answer your question: yes, the ‘semantic secret sauce' is in general due to the LLM, but leveraging those embeddings effectively requires specific architectural choices and alignment through real-world data training. This is what ConTextTab achieves, which goes beyond naïve usage of those embeddings as it would be required with GBDTs or general ICL methods such as TabPFN or TabICL.

Indeed, we observe a significant boost in performance for those baselines over the results previously reported using a fixed holdout set HPO, in line with the observations recently made in the literature [1].
In particular, ranking order now has changed for the non-semantic benchmarks, whereas the results remain conceptually unchanged in the case of the CARTE benchmark. That is, **ConTextTab sets a new standard on semantically rich datasets while performing on-par to existing approaches on non-semantic datasets**. We have also added more detailed per-benchmark analysis including win-ratios, p-values and CD diagrams, as highlighted and discussed in our answer to Rev. iSTq, further supporting our main claim. In particular, differences to TabPFN (updated to v2.1.0) on conventional benchmarks are statistically insignificant, while ConTextTab has a 94% win-rate (with a vanishingly small p-value, i.e. the difference is stat. significant) on CARTE. Moreover, we find ConTextTab does not perform significantly worse than the best-ranking model on all non-semantic benchmarks but OpenML-CTR23 (where it is however not significantly different to tuned ensembled trees).

Overall, we believe the addition of CV-ensembled baselines improves our evaluation while our core claims remain unchanged.

## Runtime evaluation
Thank you for this suggestion! As requested by other reviewers as well, **we have added a runtime analysis**. Please refer to our answer to Rev. zDEh for details and results.

## Error bars
Indeed, most results do not show confidence intervals or error bars. However, **we have added p-value matrices next to the win-ratio plots** depicted in Fig. 5 **as well as CD diagrams** in the appendix. Upon request by Rev. iSTq23, we now include this also per-benchmark, making the detailed assessment of ConTextTab performance in comparison to all evaluated baselines easier including statistical significance.

## Confusion around Eq.(2)
In the paper, we now provided a detailed architecture diagram, similar to TabICL, to show that we concatenate the queries with the induced vectors, while the remaining MAB block inputs are formed by contexts concatenated with queries. While we experimented with architectures more closely aligned with the original ISAB block used in TabICL, these resulted in lower performance. Our chosen design facilitates the propagation of query information. In each MAB block, the query rows can attend to themselves while using the custom attention matrices.

## Negative R2 scores
R2 scores are zero for naïve predictors and can be arbitrarily negative. Indeed, there are a few severe outliers in some regression tasks that are so large that they even drag the mean to be negative, which is not great. To overcome this, **we have updated all evaluation to use a soft-clipped version of R2**, smoothly transforming all negatives scores from $[-\infty, 0)$ to $[-1, 0)$ via $\tanh$ (and keeping positive scores untouched). This retains the relative ordering even of scores worse than naïve while being smoothly differentiable and less distorting to the mean. Thank you for highlighting this nuance!


## Number of parameters
The base version of our model ($n=12$, $d=768$, $d_{ff}=3072$), uses 172M parameters which reduces to 16M trainable parameters in the case of weight sharing. **We have clarified this in the paper.**

## Text embeddings
Thank you for the interesting reference, **we added a citation in the paper**!

## Minor comments
Thank you for catching those typos! Also, we’ve added TabM as a baseline and now include ModernNCA citation in the related works section. Finally, **we have added the previously lacking comment on the default context size** (which is 8k=8192)!

## Conclusion
We hope to have addressed all your concerns and are looking forward to the discussion!

### References
[1]: Erickson, et al. "TabArena: A Living Benchmark for Machine Learning on Tabular Data." arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.16791 (2025).

Thank you for reading our manuscript and providing valuable feedback! We are happy that you acknowledge our research question to be both relevant and interesting, as well as our comprehensive evaluation and well-written manuscript!

To address your concerns and questions:

## Contribution of each task to the overall evaluation
Thank you for the suggestion, **we have added CD diagrams together with win-ratio matrices and p-values for every benchmark** separately in the Appendix! This makes it much easier to assess benchmark-specific performance in addition to our main results table and strengthens our core claims!

## Skewed benchmarks 
Our main claim is that ConTextTab successfully integrates semantic information in its prediction boosting performance on semantically rich tasks. Naturally, CARTE is our main evaluation benchmark, as the remaining benchmarks contain very little semantic features. Hence, our main observation is that we perform on-par to existing ICL approaches such as TabPFN on all benchmarks other than CARTE and outperform all models on CARTE. Indeed, this remains true with the greatly improved baselines (c.f. our answer to Reviewer qbCU). Using the newly added benchmark-specific win-ratio matrix and p-values we observe that TabPFN has a win-ratio over ConTextTab ranging from 49% to 63% (excluding CARTE), however with p-values ranging from 0.09 to 0.64. Hence, the performance difference on those benchmarks is statistically insignificant. **On CARTE, ConTextTab wins over TabPFN with 94%** and a diminishing p-value, hence is statistically significantly better than TabPFN in the presence of highly semantic features.

## Benchmark inconsistencies
Thank you for pointing out the rank inconsistencies! Indeed, the Naïve rank on CARTE >11 is surprising at first, but actually correct due to a subtle nuance in the evaluation protocol: note that TabICL has partially incomplete evaluation, i.e. can be evaluated only for classification tasks. Therefore, we include it in the rankings on the classification portion of the benchmarks. Hence, for the ranking on CARTE in table 1, there are actually 12 candidates ranked, and Naïve ends up with 11.22. We then do not show the rank average of TabICL because it would only have been ranked on a subset of the tasks. We agree that this is confusing. Therefore, we have updated the tables to exclude partially evaluated models (TabICL, TabDPT, CARTE) from all ranking calculations which resolves the issue. You can find the updated results table in our answer to reviewer qbCU.


## Including more baselines
**We have added TabM** (HPO with 5-fold inner CV) and extended TabICL evaluation to all (classification) benchmarks (which was previously limited by a bug in TabICL). **We have also added Mambular** (v1.5.1), however only for CARTE and TALENT-Tiny as convergence on larger datasets was too slow to finish in time for the rebuttal. As suggested by Reviewer qbCU, **we also added tuned ensembled baselines via 5-fold inner CV**. Overall, we believe our baseline selection to be very comprehensive including all relevant conventional as well as state of the art baselines.

## Runtime comparison
Thank you for this suggestion! We have added a corresponding evaluation. As requested by other reviewers as well, **we have included a runtime analysis**. In the following, we provide the answer consistent with our response to Rev. zDEh:

We have added a runtime comparison in a controlled fashion using synthetic tables with 100 columns and varying number of training rows ranging from 1k to 10k. We synthesize data with 50% categorical/textual and 50% numeric features. We created two plots with runtime (prediction and fit + prediction) for ConTextTab, TabICL, TabPFN, XGBoost, and RealMLP for various numbers of training/context rows and one test/query row, using 5 repeats and report averages. The experiments were conducted on an H100 GPU. We find that ConTextTab is comparable to other tabular ICL models such as TabPFN and TabICL – with runtimes ranging from 0.1s up to 8s depending on the table size. As expected, due to the LLM embedding overhead, ConTextTab is typically slightly slower than TabPFN or TabICL. For ConTextTab, we observe quadratic scaling behaviors as expected due to the use of transformer backbone with memory efficient attention, however for TabPFN and TabICL it is not as noticeable, likely due to the use of flash attention. This results in ConTextTab being slower by a factor of 2 for larger context with 10k rows. While non-ICL models offer significantly faster prediction times, they require extensive training. In particular, the hyperparameter-optimized (HPO) versions of XGBoost and RealMLP exhibit fit+prediction runtimes that are two orders of magnitude higher.

## Handling of larger datasets
We point to Figure 4 in the appendix where we observe that ConTextTab, like other ICL methods, indeed struggles with very large datasets. Nevertheless, **it outperforms TabPFN also in the large-data domain**. ConTextTab handles large datasets by sampling 8k rows of context using 8-fold bagging by default which likely explains performance gains over TabPFN in this domain.

## Model code
As per NeurIPS rebuttal policy, we cannot share links (including anonymized code) during the rebuttal. We have prepared the repository and will publish the code and model checkpoints upon publication.

## Additional preprocessing strategies
We have experimented with the default standardization + linear encoding as well quantile-based binning, which are presented in the main ablation table. We have not investigated further numerical preprocessing/encoding variants, however, agree it is an interesting direction for future investigations!

## Summation of embeddings
Apologies for the confusion: embeddings are normalized via `LayerNormalization`, which was lacking from the description. We have updated the corresponding paragraph, thanks for highlighting!

## Weight sharing
Sorry, our original phrasing was unclear, and we have revised it. Our intention was to convey that the horizontal and vertical blocks use the same number of weights and are each followed by a feed-forward layer with an intermediate transformer block. This differs from TabPFNv2, where feed-forward layers are placed only after both attention blocks.

## Conclusion
We hope to have addressed all your concerns and are looking forward to the discussion!

Thank you for your feedback and acknowledging the comprehensiveness and rigor of our evaluation, as well as the conducted ablations and general approach!

To address your questions and concerns:

## Direct validation of semantic understanding
Thank you for this suggestion! While we do believe that CARTE performance showcases semantic capabilities, we agree that this is indirect and that a direct ablation would strengthen our claims. To this end, **we have conducted two semantic ablations on the CARTE benchmark** where we would expect the effect to be most pronounced:

### Semantic feature ablation
To ablate the impact of semantic embeddings of the features (string, categoricals), we evaluated the following preprocessing techniques to replace the LLM embeddings, ranging from methods that do not contain any semantics as well as conventional string encoders:

-	Using `OrdinalEncoder`, effectively replacing all string/categoricals with ordinal integer encodings, eliminating all potential semantic information,
-	Using `OrdinalEncoder` for low-cardinality and `MinHashEncoder` for high-cardinality features as a conventional method for string embeddings,
-	Using `OrdinalEncoder` for low-cardinality and `GapEncoder` encoder for high-cardinality features as another conventional method for string embeddings,
-	Using the default AutoGluon feature encoder which uses low-level NLP features for high-cardinality columns.

We compare these approaches to the default ConTextTab model with semantic LLM embeddings.

### Semantic column name ablation
Second, we investigate the impact of the semantic column name embeddings which we add to the feature embeddings.

To this end, we investigate the following two ablations:
-	Replacing the column names with `col1`, `col2`, …, `colN`. This removes any potential semantic information contained in the column names.
-	We also perform the inverse ablation: using an LLM (`gemma3-12b`), we created contextualized column descriptions for all CARTE tables by presenting the model with 5 randomly sampled rows (serialized to JSON) and asking for contextualized descriptions. We then replace all column names with `<name>:<description>` to semantically enrich them and perform prediction with ConTextTab as usual.

### Results
We find the following results, showing the base model performance and absolute changes over the base model performance for the ablated versions, which we have appended to the main ablation table in the paper:

|                                              |         |        |       |
| column semantics-add description          | **1.20**| 0.0    | 0.0   |
| column semantics-drop columnnames             | 3.35    | -1.2   | -2.1  |


Replacing LLM embeddings leads to a noticeable decline in performance, for example with accuracy dropping by ~3% and R2 score decreasing by ~5% when using ordinal encodings instead.

We also added win-ratio and p-values plots (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test) to the paper and find that the base model including semantics has a win rate of 85% to 96% over the investigated ablated models with diminishingly small p-values (therefore, statistically significant). **The model hence successfully makes use of the semantic content** inherent to categorical/string features.

Arguably, the use of column name semantics offers only slight improvements (about 1% drop in accuracy and 2% drop in R2 when __not__ using the original column names), which are however statistically significant with a win-rate of 92% over the model not using column names and a diminishing p-value. Semantically enriching column names further boost performance, though the gain is not statistically significant (with a win rate of 57% and a p-value of 0.4).

Overall, we demonstrate that **ConTextTab successfully integrates and makes use of semantics** present in the features and column names, further supporting our core claims.

## Plateauing performance after 100k training tables
We acknowledge that this behavior is not clear. We observe a significant improvement as we scale the model from `mini` to `base` size as it is indicated in the ablation section. For larger models, a few factors might contribute to the observed performance: (1) the `large` model may have been undertrained due to the limited training duration, and (2) weight sharing across many layers could become suboptimal. Such weight sharing resembles RNN unrolled in depth and deep RNNs are known to be difficult to train. We also found that removing weight sharing entirely for large models leads to unstable training, suggesting that scaling up this architecture is challenging with the training data available. Finally, part of the limitation may come from the T4 dataset itself; if the dataset lacks sufficient diversity, a relatively small subset could capture most of the signal.

## Novelty
By exhaustive evaluation and ablations, we show that our model is competitive across several established benchmarks and setting a new standard on semantically rich data, outperforming even best-in-class HPO-tuned trees and DL baselines such as TabM and RealMLP, while keeping the ICL paradigm. This is a novel and, in our opinion, a worthwhile contribution to the research field and community. While the core technical contributions of ConTextTab are relatively straight-forward, we do not consider this a weakness of our work. Moreover, certain architectural modifications, such as the clustering head designed to remove the restriction on the number of prediction classes and to incorporate target class semantics, are novel and have not yet been explored in the tabular domain.

## Limitations
We briefly discuss potential data contamination and our contamination study on CARTE but happily extend this section for clarity. With the added semantic ablation study we believe to have addressed the remaining limitations you have outlined. Throughout we make sure not to overstate the model’s performance and clearly state it’s advantage being in semantically rich tasks and benchmarks as well as its performance dependence on dataset size (as discussed in the paper and further ablated in Figure 4 in the Appendix.

## Conclusion
We hope to have addressed all your concerns and questions and are looking forward to the discussion!

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for your feedback and highlighting the comprehensiveness of our evaluation and the competitiveness of our model!

To address your concerns and questions:

## Runtime analysis
Thank you for this suggestion! **We have added a runtime comparison** in a controlled fashion using synthetic tables with 100 columns and varying number of training rows ranging from 1k to 10k. We synthesize data with 50% categorical/textual and 50% numeric features. We created two plots with runtime (prediction and fit + prediction) for ConTextTab, TabICL, TabPFN, XGBoost, and RealMLP for various numbers of training/context rows and one test/query row, using 5 repeats and report averages. The experiments were conducted on an H100 GPU. We find that ConTextTab is comparable to other tabular ICL models such as TabPFN and TabICL – with runtimes ranging from 0.1s up to 8s depending on the table size. As expected, due to the LLM embedding overhead, ConTextTab is typically slightly slower than TabPFN or TabICL. For ConTextTab, we observe quadratic scaling behaviors as expected due to the use of transformer backbone with memory efficient attention, however for TabPFN and TabICL it is not as noticeable, likely due to the use of flash attention. This results in ConTextTab being slower by a factor of 2 for larger context with 10k rows. While non-ICL models offer significantly faster prediction times, they require extensive training. In particular, the hyperparameter-optimized (HPO) versions of XGBoost and RealMLP exhibit fit+prediction runtimes that are two orders of magnitude higher.


## Dataset characteristics
We are uncertain whether this concerns the pretraining data or benchmark data used for evaluation? We provide details on the evaluation data in the appendix. Throughout, features are processed as described in the main paper, using different encoders for text, numbers, and dates in the case of ConTextTab. For all evaluated baselines, feature preprocessing is outlined in the appendix.

## Hyperparameter search space
We report the hyperparameter search space of the evaluated baselines in the appendix. For our model, we ran extensive experiments in the ablation study section in which we tried different configurations such as model size, etc., however we do not perform (algorithmic) hyperparameter optimization as is common for deep learning approaches.

## Random-weight comparison
Without any pretraining our model produces random predictions. We are unsure about the scope and goals of the suggested ablation. Note that the full model, including embedding layers and prediction heads, are (pre)trained end-to-end.

## Fine-tuning
**We have clarified the phrasing** in the ablations table.
We perform benchmark-specific finetuning to observe further downstream task improvements as a core capability of a foundation model, as similarly investigated in previous works [1, 2]. Dataset-specific fine-tuning was not effective, as the model quickly overfitted; it essentially encountered the same context at every training step.

## Summary
We hope to have clarified your questions and are looking forward to the discussion!

summary.value: This paper presents ConTextTab, a semantics-aware, table-native in-context learning (ICL) model for tabular prediction tasks. The motivation is to bridge the gap between traditional table-specific ICL architectures (e.g., TabPFN, TabICL), which excel at leveraging structural information but neglect table semantics, and large language model-based approaches (e.g., TabuLa-8B), which understand semantics but are inefficient in processing large tabular data due to linear tokenization and context limitations. ConTextTab enhances the table-native ICL backbone by introducing modality-specific embeddings for textual, numerical, and date columns, as well as semantic embeddings for column names and categorical values. The model is pretrained on large-scale real-world tabular datasets (T4), and evaluated on a suite of tabular benchmarks, demonstrating strong results—especially setting a new state-of-the-art on the semantically-rich CARTE benchmark, and exhibiting robust performance in low-data regimes. Comprehensive ablations analyze the impact of model components, context size, and data scale.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### **Strengths**

1. The experimental evaluation is comprehensive, covering 203 datasets across five different benchmarks with proper statistical analysis including critical difference diagrams. The ablation studies are thorough, examining various architectural choices, training data scales, and hyperparameter settings. The authors provide detailed implementation details and plan to release code and model weights.

2. The paper is well-written with clear motivation, methodology, and experimental setup. The figures effectively illustrate the architecture and results. The related work section provides good context for understanding the contribution relative to existing methods.

3. The multi-modal embedding approach is sensible, with appropriate handling of text, dates, and numerical features. The architectural modifications to TabPFN are well-motivated and the training procedure is clearly described.

### **Weaknesses**

1. The paper lacks direct validation of semantic understanding capabilities. There are no experiments demonstrating that the model can leverage semantic similarities between column names, understand categorical label meanings, or transfer knowledge across semantically related tasks. The "semantic understanding" claim rests primarily on downstream task performance.

2. While the combination is novel, the core technical contributions are relatively incremental. The approach primarily involves using pre-trained text embeddings and training on real data rather than synthetic data. The architectural modifications are minor adaptations of existing transformer-based designs.

questions.value:
1. Can you provide experiments that directly test semantic understanding capabilities, rather than relying solely on downstream task performance? For example, can the model correctly identify semantically similar columns across different datasets, or does it show improved performance when categorical labels have semantic meaning versus arbitrary codes? Such experiments would strengthen the core claim about semantic awareness.

2. Your results show that performance plateaus after 100K training tables and that larger models perform worse. This contradicts the intuition that semantic understanding requires large-scale data and model capacity. Can you provide a more detailed analysis of what limits further scaling and whether this indicates fundamental limitations in your approach?

limitations.value: The authors do address limitations in their conclusion section, acknowledging the challenges with scaling to large datasets and the need for more diverse semantic evaluation benchmarks. However, the limitations section could be more comprehensive. Missing discussions include potential data contamination effects, the circular reasoning in using downstream performance to validate semantic understanding, and the practical constraints of the method's applicability. The authors should also acknowledge that their evidence for semantic understanding is primarily indirect and that the method's advantages may be limited to specific data regimes and domains.

summary.value:
The authors introduce ConTextTab, a new tabular ICL model, following the ideas presented in TabPFN. The core differences are pre-training on real world data as well as integrating semantic understanding (column names, etc.) into the model.
The core training architecture of common ICL models (TabPFN, TabICL, Attic) is still implemented.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strength
- Well written
- Relevant and interesting research question addressing the problems of current ICL models to adequately be applied to real-world datasets
- Benchmarks are very large

# Weaknesses
- Benchmarks are somewhat skewed. It seems as if ConTextTab is outperforming PFN only on the CARTE benchmark whereas TabPFN outperforms ConTextTab on all other benchmarks. 
  - I am not sure how  in Table 1 Naive in the CARTE benchmark can have an average rank > 11 when you compare 11 models? This somehow makes me question the ranks reported for CARTE since they are so different from all other tasks (even TabReD). And why does TabICL not have a rank if you have an accuracy?
- While the benchmarks are quite large, including TabM [1], Mambular [2] and extending TabICL [3] to further datasets would have been nice.
- Compute times for different models, especially for TabPFN, TabICL and ConTextTab are missing.
- While mentioning the dataset sizes of TabPFN and TabICL as limitations, I did not find any information of whether ConTextTab can handle larger datasets any better than the two. The results on the TabReD dataset suggest otherwise.

# General comment
- Section 3.4 is somewhat poorly named. Currently I would read it as an alternative idea to your presented architecture.




------

[1] Gorishniy, Yury, Akim Kotelnikov, and Artem Babenko. "TabM: Advancing tabular deep learning with parameter-efficient ensembling." The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations.          
[2] Thielmann, Anton Frederik, et al. "Mambular: A sequential model for tabular deep learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2408.06291 (2024).        
[3] Qu, Jingang, et al. "TabICL: A Tabular Foundation Model for In-Context Learning on Large Data." arXiv preprint arXiv:2502.05564 (2025).

questions.value:
- Please release model code during reviews in an anonymous format.
- Could you outline the contributions of each task to the total number of datasets.
  - Provide critical difference diagrams for each benchmark suite separately
- Have you tried out different preprocessing strategies, especially for numerical, i.e. PLE or PLR?
- Why do you actually sum the embeddings? Wouldn't at least averaging them be more secure as o avoid overly large values?

In section 3.2 you write that "horizontal" and "vertical" blocks have exactly the same weights. Could you elaborate? Do they share the weights?

summary.value: The paper introduces ConTextTab, a foundation model for tabular data using in-context learning that is pre-trained on real tables and has meta-learned how to handle not only numerical and categorical features but also text, dates, and column names. ConTextTab combines architectural innovations of different models together with mechanisms for handling embeddings of different column types. It is evaluated on multiple benchmarks with a diverse set of baselines and achieves strong results, particularly on the semantically rich CARTE benchmark, where it sets a new state-of-the art. Numerous ablations illustrate the effect of different design decisions.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- Clarity: The paper is well-written and generally easy to follow. 
- Significance: The paper studies a practically important problem. It provides many interesting insights into the pre-training and architecture of tabular foundation models, therefore I expect that it will be significant for the development of future models. In particular, I appreciate the numerous ablations.
- The paper includes a diverse set of established baselines.
- The paper is not overselling too much. In particular, I appreciate that the paper includes multiple benchmarks, both textual and non-textual ones, which is not common for papers introducing textual models.

Weaknesses:

(1) The paper compares foundation models using training+validation data in the forward pass to non-foundation models that (mostly) use a single train-val holdout split (according to Appendix B.2). The classical methods would likely benefit significantly from inner cross-validation (e.g., 8-fold as in AutoGluon, but 5-fold is also common), while the foundation models would probably not benefit from it compared to the current approach. This is a major concern for my score. I see several approaches to address this, listed in order of decreasing quality: (a) Ideally the authors would run every of the non-foundation methods with cross-validation. However, I understand that this is expensive. (One way to illustrate the cost would be to actually report the training+inference costs of different models.) (b) If the authors want to keep the holdout validation, in my experience it would at least be more fair to compare to foundation models that only see the training set. (One might think that this is now unfair to the foundation models as they don't see the validation set at all, but other models can benefit a lot from cross-validation due to the ensembling, while foundation models are already ensembled.) This of course makes the comparison of foundation models to AutoGluon unfair, so it might be best to have a train+val and a train version of the foundation models. (c) Mention this point in the main paper and state it as a limitation.

(2) The runtime (training+inference) of methods is not evaluated, making it unclear how fast ConTextTab is compared to other models.

(3) Minor: Most results come without error bars.


Originality: The proposed method is partially a combination of aspects of different models (dataset from TabuLa, base architecture from TabPFNv2, etc.) with some new aspects in terms of the details and the handling of different datatypes. I see originality as neither a strength nor weakness of the paper.

questions.value:
- Eq. (2): I find this part somewhat confusing. In TabICL, if I understand correctly, only the final MAB uses Q, so wouldn't it be MAB(C+Q, MAB(I, C))? A diagram as in TabICL might help to illustrate things. Also, in MAB(X, Y), it could be clarified that X are the queries and Y are the keys.
- Figure 2: Why is the R2 score of CatBoost [HPO] negative on OML-CTR23?
- How many parameters does the model have, and how does it compare to the other foundation models?
- For the text embedding models, the authors might want to look into / cite https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09634


Minor comments:
- l. 69: could mention TabM and ModernNCA as well
- l. 109: "then" -> "than"
- l. 292: It could be nice to state the default context size (8c = 7600 if I understand correctly)
- l. 536: "deault" -> "default"
- l. 580: "." missing

limitations.value: The paper states quite a few limitations. Besides the mentioned lack of (inner) cross-validation, there are some other concerns that affect tabular benchmarks in general and could be discussed, like dataset quality, quality of search spaces for baselines, etc.

final_justification.value:
Overall, I really like the paper, and I am hesitant between scoring it a 5 or a 6.
- Evaluation: The authors have addressed all of my concerns by running baselines with cross-validation, adding time experiments, adding more baselines (TabM), better search spaces, etc. I think the evaluation is strong, and it contains multiple benchmarks highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of the model. In the case of the CARTE benchmark, it is a bit unclear how to best preprocess strings for the baselines - the authors have taken a solid choice, but it is unclear from the literature what is the best choice.
- The model is state-of-the-art on the CARTE benchmark by a margin. It is a bit worse than the baselines on purely numerical/categorical benchmarks, but I think compared to many other papers that wouldn't have included these benchmarks or would have used weaker baselines, this is still pretty strong.
- I like that the paper includes many ablations on model design.

title.value: ConTextTab: A Semantics-Aware Tabular In-Context Learner

TLDR.value: A state-of-the-art semantics-enriched TabPFNv2-style in-context learner trained on real-world tabular data

abstract.value: Tabular in-context learning (ICL) has recently achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on several tabular prediction tasks. Previously restricted to classification problems on small tables, recent advances such as TabPFN and TabICL have extended its use to larger datasets. Although current table-native ICL architectures are architecturally efficient and well-adapted to tabular data structures, their exclusive training on synthetic data limits their ability to fully leverage the rich semantics and world knowledge contained in real-world tabular data. At the other end of the spectrum, tabular ICL models based on pretrained large language models such as TabuLa-8B integrate deep semantic understanding and world knowledge but are only able to make use of a small amount of context due to inherent architectural limitations. With the aim to combine the best of both these worlds, we introduce ConTextTab, integrating semantic understanding and alignment into a table-native ICL framework. By employing specialized embeddings for different data modalities and by training on large-scale real-world tabular data, our model is competitive with SOTA across a broad set of benchmarks while setting a new standard on the semantically rich CARTE benchmark. Code and model checkpoints are available at: https://github.com/SAP-samples/contexttab .

Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).
